claims.text: The target nanoparticles contain five or more metals in approximately equiatomic ratios and begin as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability over 473–1923 K is governed primarily by kinetically limited differential atomic diffusion and surface segregation.
Reactive reducing or oxidizing atmospheres accelerate differential diffusion and surface segregation relative to inert atmospheres.
High mixing entropy alone is not the primary determinant of stability under operating conditions.
Increasing temperature raises atomic mobility and enables differential diffusion among constituent metals.
The constituent elements can undergo element-specific redox interactions in a reactive atmosphere.
Element-specific redox interactions further promote atomic diffusion.
Reactive-atmosphere-enhanced diffusion causes selected elements to segregate at nanoparticle surfaces.
Reactive-atmosphere-enhanced diffusion can produce intermetallic domains.
Kinetic effects can overcome entropy-related thermodynamic stabilization of the homogeneous alloy.
Under inert conditions, kinetic barriers maintain the mixed single-phase structure.
Nanoparticles annealed under inert atmosphere will largely retain a homogeneous single-phase structure across the tested range.
Nanoparticles treated under reducing or oxidizing atmospheres will exhibit more elemental segregation than inert-atmosphere controls.
Reactive-atmosphere treatment may produce secondary phases or intermetallic ordering.
Segregation and phase changes will become more pronounced as temperature increases within 473–1923 K.
The onset temperature and atmosphere dependence of instability vary with alloy composition and particle size.
Synthesis method, particle-size distribution, and extreme compositions can alter the balance between kinetic and thermodynamic stabilization.

contradictions.description: The material and baseline are described as homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles, whereas the falsification design calls the synthesized nanoparticles 'heterogeneous' while simultaneously requiring them to be a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
